html:
The Yolngu are a group of Aboriginal Australian peoples of northeast Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory. Yolngu means "person" in their languages. The map shows them from 1600 to 1800.

Every Yolngu clan belongs to one of two halves, or moieties, called Dhuwa and Yirritja, and the moieties shape marriage, ceremony and law. Their homeland gave the world the yidaki, better known as the didgeridoo, and a tradition of bark painting with fine crosshatched designs.

From the 1700s until 1906, fishing fleets from Makassar in Sulawesi came each wet season to gather sea cucumber, the Makassan trepang trade. The visitors left words, tools and stories in Yolngu culture.

In 1963 Yolngu leaders at Yirrkala sent the Yirrkala bark petitions to the federal Parliament, protesting a bauxite mine on their land. Their later court case lost in 1971, but it fed the national campaign for land rights. The band Yothu Yindi brought Yolngu music to a wide audience in the 1990s. Neighbours on the map include the Ngandi and the Nunggubuyu. See Aboriginal Australian societies.
